title: Why Saudi Just Abandoned Its Core Oil Rule | OilPrice.com

Simon Watkins is a former senior FX trader and salesman, financial journalist, and best-selling author. He was Head of Forex Institutional Sales and Trading for…

Few could argue with U.S. President Donald Trump’s key objective in launching ‘Operation Epic Fury’ against Iran on 28 February -- to prevent Iran from ever being able to develop a nuclear weapon. All members of his Cabinet fully backed this aim at the time, as they did the other three: to effect regime change, to critically degrade Iran’s ballistic missile capability, and to neutralise the ability of its proxies, especially Hamas and Hezbollah, to cause mayhem across the Middle East and the world. The degree to which these objectives have been achieved so far is a matter for debate, but what is not is that Washington’s closest Arab allies now harbour deep misgivings over America’s ability to shield them from the Iranian hornet’s nest that U.S. attacks have provoked. This has again made them more susceptible to the soothing assurances from Beijing that it can keep them safe from the terror of Tehran over the long term. This situation, in turn, threatens Trump’s ‘Abraham Accords’ plan that lay at the heart of his Middle East foreign policy, as fully examined in my latest book on the new global oil market order. Several recent moves by leading Middle East power Saudi Arabia underline this threat.

The most recent was the announcement from Saudi oil and gas flagship Aramco that it and the Kingdom are seeking to partner with other countries to expand their strategic oil stockpile. Despite the perennial taking up of its crude production capabilities to boost its global profile over the years, Saudi Arabia’s average oil output from 1973 to yesterday is 8.295 million barrels per day (bpd), and it is currently around 8 million bpd. That said, Saudi expects oil demand to bounce when the war ends and is also working on alternative export routes to circumvent the likely ongoing Iranian threat around the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab Strait and Suez Canal. Perhaps the single-most strategically important component of this effort to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz remains the long-planned but now dynamically expedited India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC). Originally launched at the 2023 G20 Summit but stalled by regional conflict, the project has been turbocharged by the Strait of Hormuz blockade, with planners now estimating it could eventually divert around 60 percent of container traffic that historically has transited the Strait of Hormuz. Its architecture is built around two integrated corridors: an eastern maritime leg linking India’s western ports to the Arabian Gulf, and a northern overland rail network running through Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel’s Port of Haifa, from where short?sea shipping connects directly to Europe. Crucially, the 2026 wartime redesign anchors the eastern maritime leg in Oman rather than the UAE, allowing ships from India to unload entirely outside the Strait of Hormuz before transferring cargo onto the Arabian Peninsula rail grid. Additional ‘IMEC Plus’ nodes through Egypt and Syria are under discussion to create a wider lattice of land?based alternatives, while new legal frameworks -- including the India–European Union (EU) free trade agreement and the U.S. Senate’s ‘Eastern Mediterranean Gateway Act’ -- have formally designated Greece as Europe’s entry hub, a very senior source inside the EU’s security complex exclusively told OilPrice.com. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is eyeing the expansion of its East-West Pipeline (1,200 km long, moving crude from eastern oil fields across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu) to 10 million bpd within the next two to three years. Saudi Arabia’s desire to partner with other countries to expand its strategic oil stockpile marks a seismic shift in policy. Historically, the Kingdom responded to oil demand spikes by simply pumping more crude from its domestic oilfields, drawing down from its own domestic storage, or securing barrels in the international spot and forward markets. However, this announcement signals that Saudi Arabia can no longer rely solely on its own geography and security to guarantee oil delivery. By seeking access to the strategic, government-owned stockpiles of foreign nations -- particularly in Asia -- Aramco wants to double its overseas storage capacity. That necessitates moving enormous volumes of Saudi oil out of the volatile Gulf region ahead of time and placing it directly into the backyards of its biggest customers. In other words, the Saudis are saying that the physical infrastructure inside the Middle East is too exposed to rely on exclusively, and to ensure seamless supplies in the future, they are transitioning from a model of ‘we will get it when you need it’ to ‘we will store millions of barrels in your country so a local drone strike cannot trigger a global economic collapse.’ In fact, the first such deal was quickly struck by Saudi Arabia on 26 October to store crude oil at Singapore’s Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027. The caverns can store up to 1.47 million cubic metres of liquid hydrocarbons such as crude oil and condensate.

Whilst sensibly pragmatic on Saudi Arabia’s part, given recent events, this general strategy is disastrous for the U.S.’s image in the Middle East. In recent years, Saudi Arabia has consistently spent tens of billions of dollars annually on American-sourced defence systems, with historical and recent baseline arms agreements valued at roughly USD75 billion a year. While Riyadh has recently allocated roughly USD83 billion per year to its total national defence budget, the U.S. remains its primary provider, accounting for nearly 80 percent of all Saudi weapons imports.
